title: Food & Cooking Shorts · Episode 1
chapters: Chocolate: from bitter drink to sweet bar
Coffee: from goat legend to flat white

units.t: Food & Cooking Shorts. Episode one.
In this episode: Bananas: the fruit of clones, Bush foods: Australia's native pantry, Chocolate: from bitter drink to sweet bar and Coffee: from goat legend to flat white.
Part one. Bananas: the fruit of clones.
The banana in your lunchbox is almost certainly a genetic copy of nearly every other banana in the shop.
That makes it cheap, convenient and surprisingly fragile.
Not a tree, a berry.
A banana plantation looks like a forest, but banana plants are not trees.
They have no wood.
What looks like a trunk is a pseudostem of tightly wrapped leaf bases, and the true stem stays mostly underground as a fleshy corm.
Some plants grow taller than a house, making them among the largest herbaceous plants in the world.
Each pseudostem flowers once, bears one large bunch and dies back, while new shoots called suckers rise from the base.
Botanically, the fruit is a berry, because it develops from a single flower's ovary and has its seeds inside the flesh.
Strawberries, confusingly, do not count as true berries.
Seedless clones.
Wild bananas, which grow across South-East Asia and the western Pacific, are full of hard seeds.
Evidence from Kuk Swamp in Papua New Guinea suggests people cultivated bananas there around 7,000 years ago.
Traders and migrants carried them to India, Africa and the Pacific, and they reached the Americas after European contact in the early sixteenth century.
Sweet bananas are eaten raw, while plantains and cooking bananas are boiled or fried, and in parts of East Africa they are a daily staple.
Our bananas come from rare plants with three sets of chromosomes, which makes them sterile.
The dark specks inside are undeveloped seeds.
Farmers plant suckers, cuttings or laboratory plantlets, so each plant is identical to its parent.
Big Mike to Cavendish.
Until the mid-twentieth century, the banana in Western shops was mostly the Gros Michel, or Big Mike.
It was large and creamy, and its thick skin survived long shipping.
But it was vulnerable to Panama disease, a wilt caused by a soil fungus that blocks the plant's water vessels and can persist in soil for decades.
Every Gros Michel was a clone, so none had resistance.
Plantations across Central America and the Caribbean were devastated.
By the 1960s, exporters had switched to the Cavendish, which resisted that strain.
The Cavendish has an English story.
In the 1830s, the Duke of Devonshire's gardener Joseph Paxton, who later designed the Crystal Palace, coaxed one into fruit in the Chatsworth House hothouses and named it after his employer.
It was more delicate, so exporters began packing bananas in boxes.
How bananas ripen.
Shop bananas are harvested hard and green, because ripe fruit bruises easily.
Like apples, tomatoes and avocados, bananas are climacteric fruit: they keep ripening after picking.
The trigger is ethylene, a simple gas the fruit produces itself.
Distributors use ripening rooms and add a little ethylene to start the fruit off evenly.
As a banana ripens, starch converts to sugars, the flesh softens and the green chlorophyll in the skin breaks down, revealing yellow pigments.
Brown spots mean it is very ripe.
A paper bag with an apple traps ethylene and speeds ripening, while refrigeration blackens the skin but leaves the flesh fine.
Power and Australian bananas.
In the early twentieth century, American companies such as United Fruit owned plantations, railways and ports in Central America.
Henry used the phrase "banana republic" for a country dominated by foreign business.
In 1928 Colombian troops fired on striking banana workers, and in 1954 a CIA-backed coup removed Guatemala's elected government, whose land reforms threatened United Fruit.
Most Australian bananas grow in far north Queensland, around Tully and Innisfail.
Cavendish dominates, and the small, sweet Lady Finger is a local favourite.
Fresh bananas are not imported, so cyclones such as Larry in 2006 and Yasi in 2011 sent prices soaring.
The biggest threat is Tropical Race 4, a Panama disease strain that attacks Cavendish and was found in Queensland in 2015.
The key idea: The banana plant is a giant herb with a trunk made of leaves, and its fruit is botanically a berry.
Part two. Bush foods: Australia's native pantry.
Long before supermarkets, this continent was a pantry of seeds, fruits, nuts and greens known intimately by First Nations peoples.
Many are now finding their way onto restaurant menus.
Food knowledge and flour.
Early Europeans assumed the land offered little to eat.
They were badly mistaken.
Over tens of thousands of years, First Nations peoples learned which plants and animals were edible, when they ripened, how to prepare them and how to look after the places they grew.
That knowledge differed from Country to Country and was tied to seasons, ceremony, law and trade.
Bush foods were never lost to the communities who knew them.
In the dry inland, seeds were winnowed, ground between stones, mixed with water and baked as cakes in hot ashes.
Grinding stones tens of thousands of years old are among the oldest evidence of seed grinding anywhere.
That suggests bread-making long before farming began in the Middle East.
Native flavours.
Wattleseed comes from certain acacias, the wattles whose golden flowers are Australia's floral emblem.
Roasted and ground, it tastes nutty, like coffee, chocolate and hazelnut, and turns up in bread, ice cream and desserts.
Only particular species are used for food and some acacias are toxic, so do not experiment alone.
Lemon myrtle is a Queensland rainforest tree whose leaves are packed with citral, the compound behind lemon scent.
Many people find it more lemony than lemon itself, and it flavours teas, biscuits, marinades and cheesecakes.
Pepperberry and pepperleaf, from Tasmanian mountain pepper, add a hot, spicy bite that some cooks use instead of black pepper.
Fruits and greens.
The finger lime grows wild in rainforest near the New South Wales and Queensland border.
Slice one open and tiny pearls of juice tumble out, earning the nickname 'citrus caviar'.
Chefs love it with seafood.
The quandong, or desert peach, has tart red flesh used in jams and pies, and its hard seed was used for jewellery and games.
The Kakadu plum, or gubinge, from northern Australia, has one of the highest vitamin C contents of any fruit, and Aboriginal communities have harvested it for generations.
Warrigal greens grow along coasts and were eaten by Captain Cook's crew to ward off scurvy.
They contain oxalates, so blanch them briefly before eating.
Nuts and gatherings.
The macadamia is Australia's most successful native food crop.
Its trees come from rainforest in south-east Queensland and northern New South Wales, where Aboriginal people had long eaten the nuts.
Ironically, the first big industry grew in Hawaii in the twentieth century, from Australian trees, and many assumed the nut was Hawaiian.
Genetic research suggests most Hawaiian commercial trees descend from a very small number of Queensland trees.
That narrow base makes the crop vulnerable to disease, and several wild species are now threatened.
In the Bunya Mountains of Queensland, bunya pines drop huge cones of starchy nuts.
In heavy years many Aboriginal groups travelled long distances to feast, hold ceremonies, trade, arrange marriages and settle disputes.
Respect and first tastes.
The native food industry has grown quickly, but research has found that only a small share of it is owned or led by First Nations people, even though it rests on their knowledge.
Many communities and organisations are working to change that, through Aboriginal-owned businesses, fair partnerships and protections for traditional knowledge.
Look for products that name the communities involved or come from Indigenous-owned enterprises.
Foraging without expert knowledge is risky, because some native plants are toxic or need careful preparation.
Buy from reputable suppliers, and learn from First Nations guides where possible.
For an easy first taste, try a pinch of wattleseed in pancakes or lemon myrtle in a cup of tea.
The key idea: First Nations peoples built deep knowledge of native foods over tens of thousands of years, including early seed grinding.
Part three. Chocolate: from bitter drink to sweet bar.
For thousands of years, chocolate was a frothy, bitter drink for rulers and gods.
It became the solid, sweet bar we know only in the last two centuries.
Food of the gods.
Chocolate begins with the cacao tree, Theobroma cacao, meaning 'food of the gods'.
It is native to the tropical Americas, and traces of cacao on pottery in Ecuador are more than 5,000 years old.
The Olmec, Maya and Aztec peoples made it central to their cultures.
They ate no chocolate bars.
They ground roasted beans into a paste, mixed it with water, often added chilli, maize or flowers, and poured the drink from a height to raise a prized foam.
It was bitter, not sweet, and featured in ceremonies, feasts and marriages.
The Aztecs valued the beans so highly that they used them as money.
Sugar, slavery and farms.
Spanish invaders met cacao in the sixteenth century and took it home.
Europeans found the bitter drink strange until it was sweetened with sugar and spiced with cinnamon and vanilla.
It became a luxury for royal courts and the wealthy.
Because sugar and cacao came from colonial plantations, the taste was tied to the forced labour of enslaved people.
Cacao needs hot, humid land near the equator.
Today most grows in West Africa, with Cote d'Ivoire and Ghana producing well over half of global supply, mostly on small family farms.
Many farmers earn very little, and investigations have repeatedly found child labour.
Certification schemes help, with mixed results.
When harvests failed in 2023 and 2024, prices hit records and bars grew dearer or smaller.
How the bar was invented.
Modern chocolate is surprisingly recent.
In 1828 the Dutch van Houten family patented a press that squeezed much of the fat, cocoa butter, from ground cacao, leaving a powder that mixed easily into drinks.
The cocoa butter proved useful.
In 1847 the English firm J.
S.
Fry and Sons combined cocoa powder, sugar and extra cocoa butter into a mouldable paste, often called the first modern chocolate bar.
In the 1870s Swiss maker Daniel Peter added condensed milk, with help from his neighbour Henri Nestle, to create milk chocolate.
Soon after, Rodolphe Lindt invented the conche, a machine that stirs chocolate for hours or days, making it far smoother than the gritty bars before it.
Pod, bean and temper.
Cacao pods grow straight from the trunk, each holding dozens of beans in sweet white pulp.
Farmers pile the beans and pulp, often under banana leaves, for several days.
Yeasts and bacteria feast on the pulp, the pile heats up, and chemical changes build chocolate flavour.
Without fermentation cacao tastes astringent and flat.
The beans are dried, roasted, cracked and winnowed into nibs, which are ground into cocoa mass.
It is also called cocoa liquor, but contains no alcohol.
Cocoa butter can set into several crystal forms, and only one gives a glossy, snapping bar.
Tempering, heating, cooling and gently reheating, forms the right crystals.
Poorly tempered chocolate may show white or grey bloom, which is cocoa butter or sugar on the surface.
It looks unappealing but is safe to eat.
Health, treats and pets.
Cacao contains flavanols, studied for possible benefits to blood vessels, and theobromine, a mild stimulant related to caffeine.
Headlines sometimes call chocolate a health food.
In reality most chocolate is high in sugar and fat, and processing can strip out many flavanols, so enjoy it as a treat.
This is general information, and healthdirect is a good place for dietary advice.
One warning matters.
Dogs break down theobromine far more slowly than people, so chocolate can poison them.
Dark chocolate and cooking chocolate are the most dangerous.
If a dog eats chocolate, call a vet promptly, especially around Easter and Christmas.
The key idea: For thousands of years cacao was a bitter, frothy drink in the Americas, not a sweet bar.
Part four. Coffee: from goat legend to flat white.
Every morning, billions of people drink the roasted seeds of a cherry from the Ethiopian highlands.
Here is how that seed conquered the world, and what actually happens between the farm and your cup.
Ethiopia, Yemen, two species.
The tale of Kaldi, an Ethiopian goatherd whose goats pranced after eating red berries, is charming but only legend.
It was first written down centuries after it supposedly happened.

What we know is that arabica grows wild in Ethiopia's highland forests, and that the first solid evidence of people drinking coffee comes from fifteenth-century Yemen, where Sufi communities brewed it to stay awake for night prayers.
It spread from the port of Mocha, whose name lives on in cafe menus.
Arabica is sweeter and more complex but fussy about heat.
Robusta is hardier, more bitter and has roughly twice the caffeine, so it adds body and crema to espresso blends.
Brazil leads production by far, with Vietnam usually second.
The social drink.
By the sixteenth century, coffeehouses thrived in Cairo and Istanbul, and some rulers tried to ban them, worried by the gossip and political talk.
In seventeenth-century London they were nicknamed 'penny universities': for the price of a cup you could read newspapers and argue with strangers for hours.
Merchants and ship owners met at Edward Lloyd's coffeehouse to swap shipping news, and it grew into Lloyd's of London.
Unlike beer and wine, coffee sharpened people rather than dulling them.
Australia was a tea country, and coffee often meant instant, until Italian and Greek migrants opened cafes with espresso machines after the Second World War.
The flat white followed, though New Zealanders claim it too.
From cherry to green bean.
Coffee grows as small cherries that ripen from green to deep red.
Each usually holds two seeds, the beans.
After picking, the fruit must be removed, and the method matters.
In washed processing, the skin and most of the sticky flesh are stripped off and microbes break down the rest, giving clean, bright flavours.
In natural processing, the whole cherry is dried in the sun first, which can add fruity, wine-like notes.
Either way you end up with a hard, pale green bean that smells grassy, nothing like coffee.
Green beans keep well for months, so coffee travels the world in this state and is roasted closer to where it is drunk.
The magic of roasting.
Roasting is where flavour is created.
Green beans tumble in hot air, usually reaching around 200 degrees Celsius.
They dry out and turn yellow, smelling a little like bread.
Then sugars caramelise, and amino acids react with sugars in the Maillard reaction, the same chemistry that browns toast and seared steak.
Pressure builds until the beans crack audibly, rather like popcorn.
Scientists have found hundreds of aroma compounds in roasted coffee.
Light roasts keep more of the bean's origin character, often fruity or floral and more acidic.
Dark roasts taste of the roast itself: smoky, bitter and chocolatey.
Roasted beans go stale within weeks as aromas escape, so freshness matters.
Brewing is extraction.
Whatever your method, brewing is extraction: water dissolves flavour from ground coffee.
Acids dissolve first, then sweeter compounds, and bitter ones last.
Too little extraction tastes sour and thin; too much turns harsh and bitter.
Grind size, water temperature, contact time and the coffee-to-water ratio are your levers.
Espresso forces hot water through very fine grounds at about nine bars for roughly half a minute, making a small, intense shot topped with crema.
Plunger coffee steeps coarse grounds for several minutes.
Cold brew steeps for many hours, giving a smoother, less acidic drink.
Caffeine works by blocking adenosine, which makes us sleepy.
This is general information, so check healthdirect for caffeine limits.
The key idea: Coffee has real roots in Ethiopia and Yemen, and two species, arabica and robusta, supply almost all the world's coffee.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why is a banana plant not a tree?
Answer. It has no wood; its trunk is wrapped leaf bases.
Question two. What do very old Australian grinding stones suggest?
Answer. People ground seed flour here very early.
Question three. How did the Maya and Aztecs usually enjoy cacao?
Answer. As a bitter, frothy, spiced drink.
Question four. How does robusta differ from arabica?
Answer. It is hardier and more bitter, with about twice the caffeine.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
